newsitem.title: FRANCE: French soccer tycoon goes on stockmarket.
newsitem.headline: French soccer tycoon goes on stockmarket.

text.p: Jean-Claude Darmon, dubbed the superintendent of French soccer, announced on Tuesday his group would be quoted on the Paris stockmarket from December 5..
The move reflected the meteoric financial growth of French soccer in recent years.

Shares will be made available at 215 francs ($40) and the 55-year-old Darmon, who started his career in French soccer in 1968 by publishing a yearly summary of the domestic league season, said he hoped 15 percent of the group's capital would be held by the public..
The group's turnover, 28 years after its creation, was estimated at 652 million francs ($120 million) last June..
Darmon told a press conference his decision to try his luck at the bourse reflected "a need for recognition and a wish to expand his groupps activities abroad"..
The Darmon group boasts it is the European leader in sports communications.
It is in charge of the communication budgets of ten French first division clubs and also negotiates television broadcasting and publicity rights for the French National League (LNF)..
Darmon added he hoped to become the world leader in sports communication. Some 76 percent of the group's turnover comes from France, and 89 percent from soccer.
Darmon's move came just as the LNF announced its finances were sound for the second season running in 1996 after seasons marred by bankrupcies and financial scandals..
On Saturday, LNF president Noel Le Graet said the league had made a 655,000 francs profit despite pouring 419 million francs of its revenue back into clubs..
European Cup Winner'p Cup holders Paris St-Germain, one of the 10 clubs in Darmon's group, had the biggest budget in the French first division last season with 338.1 million francs, Le Graet said.
It made PSG the 22nd wealthiest club in Europe..
When Le Graet took over in 1991, the overall debts of French professional teams was estimated at over 600 million francs.
A series of scandals marked the sudden intrusion of big money in French soccer ten years ago.
Clubs like Bordeaux, Toulon, Brest and even former European champions Marseille went into receivership or were relegated to lower divisions for financial problems.
